findings.title: Legacy router can return a nil *Route with a nil error
findings.impact: FindRoute can fall through its error branches while `route` is still nil and return (nil, pathParams, nil). Every caller treats a nil error as success and immediately dereferences the route - openapi3filter.ValidateRequest reads route.Operation, route.PathItem and route.Spec at validate_request.go:41-51 - so the caller panics with a nil-pointer dereference. It is reachable when the trie holds a node whose Value is not a *routers.Route, which is exactly what AddRoute stores (it puts the *Router in the node, not a Route), while the path also exists in doc.Paths with a matching operation.

findings.title: Request and response bodies are read fully into memory with no size limit
findings.impact: ValidateRequestBody buffers the entire request body with io.ReadAll and then keeps a second copy for the replayable GetBody, so peak memory is at least twice the body size per in-flight request, before the application handler has seen a single byte. validateSecurityRequirement does the same a second time. ValidateResponse buffers the whole response body likewise, and the strict/warn response wrappers buffer it again. Nothing in the library caps any of this and no option exists to cap it, so a handful of concurrent large uploads can exhaust process memory. The multipart decoder compounds it: it loops over parts with no limit on part count or aggregate size and accumulates every decoded part in a map.

findings.title: Global compiled-pattern cache ignores the configured RegexCompiler, silently bypassing a custom regex engine
findings.impact: Options.RegexCompiler / SetSchemaRegexCompiler exist so an operator can substitute a different regular-expression implementation - typically one with an execution budget, a step limit, or ECMA-262 semantics - for schema `pattern` checks. The cache lookup is keyed only on the pattern text, with no notion of which compiler produced the entry. Whichever compiler wins the race for a given pattern string wins for the whole process: a pattern first compiled by Go's regexp is thereafter used even for callers that asked for the custom engine, and a pattern first compiled by the custom engine is used for callers that did not. The mitigation the operator configured is therefore not applied, and behaviour differs run to run depending on which request arrives first.

findings.title: Unchecked type assertions on x- extension values panic while converting a hostile Swagger 2.0 document
findings.impact: The v2->v3 converter reads two extension keys and asserts their type without checking. A document that supplies x-formData-name or x-originalParamName as anything other than a string (a number, a list, an object - all valid YAML/JSON) panics the converting goroutine. For any service that converts user-supplied Swagger documents this is a trivial unauthenticated crash; the panic is not recovered anywhere in the package.

findings.title: Unchecked type assertion in deepSet panics on conflicting deepObject query keys (unauthenticated remote panic)
findings.impact: Any request that reaches a query parameter declared with style: deepObject can crash the validation call with 'interface conversion: interface {} is string, not map[string]interface {}'. The panic happens inside the library, before the application handler runs, so no application-level input check can prevent it. Under net/http the request is aborted and the connection torn down; in any embedding that does not have a recover() on the path (worker, gRPC gateway, Lambda/FaaS handler, custom server, or a goroutine spawned by the caller) the process dies. It is trivially repeatable, so it is a cheap unauthenticated denial of service.

findings.title: OpenAPI version handling is a hardcoded allowlist; unknown patch versions silently disable 3.1 validation
findings.impact: OpenAPIMajorMinor recognises a fixed list of literal version strings. A document declaring a version outside that list - e.g. openapi: 3.1.3 or 3.2.1 - returns the empty string, so IsOpenAPI30 and IsOpenAPI31OrLater are both false. T.Validate does not reject an unrecognised version (it only rejects an empty one), so such a document loads; but openapi3filter then never applies EnableJSONSchema2020, and the 3.1-only keywords are handled by the 3.0 engine that ignores them. The document is neither rejected as unsupported nor validated as 3.1 - it is validated as something weaker, silently. The same allowlist means every future patch release of the specification requires a code change to be handled at all.

findings.title: Validation errors embed the full schema and the offending request value, and DefaultErrorEncoder writes them to the HTTP response
findings.impact: By default SchemaError.Error() appends the complete JSON of the failing schema and the complete rejected value. ValidationHandler installs DefaultErrorEncoder unless the embedder overrides it, and DefaultErrorEncoder writes err.Error() straight into the response body. A client that sends a bad request therefore receives (a) the internal schema definition - property names, formats, patterns, enum members, min/max bounds - which is an API-surface map for an attacker, and (b) a verbatim echo of its own submitted value. When the failing field is a credential, token, or other secret carried in the body, that secret is echoed back and, because the same string is what the Validator middleware hands to logFunc, it is also written to the application log. Note that RequestError does not implement StatusCoder, so DefaultErrorEncoder answers these with HTTP 500 rather than 400, mislabelling client input errors as server faults.

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation silently falls back to the 3.0 engine when the 2020-12 schema fails to compile (fail-open)
findings.impact: For OpenAPI 3.1+ documents, openapi3filter enables the JSON Schema 2020-12 validator. If building that validator returns any error, the code silently reverts to the built-in visitJSON engine, which implements none of the 2020-12 keywords: prefixItems, contains/minContains/maxContains, patternProperties, propertyNames, dependentSchemas, dependentRequired, if/then/else, unevaluatedItems and unevaluatedProperties are simply ignored there. Constraints the API author wrote are then not enforced at all, and nothing is logged or returned to signal the downgrade - the request is reported as valid. Any authorisation or safety property expressed with those keywords (e.g. propertyNames restricting which fields a caller may set, or if/then requiring a field only for privileged payloads) is bypassed.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder decompresses without any limit (zip bomb)
findings.impact: The decoder buffers the whole request body, opens it as a zip archive, and concatenates every entry's fully decompressed contents into one in-memory string with no cap on entry count, per-entry size, or total output. A small archive with a very high compression ratio expands to arbitrary memory and kills the process. It is not registered by default, so it only affects deployments that opt in via RegisterBodyDecoder - which is why this is rated low rather than higher.

findings.title: JSON Schema 2020-12 validator is rebuilt and recompiled on every validation call
findings.impact: For any OpenAPI 3.1+ document, each request body, each response body, each parameter and each response header validated by openapi3filter marshals the schema to JSON, unmarshals it into a generic map, walks and mutates that map, creates a fresh jsonschema.Compiler, registers format validators and compiles the schema from scratch. Nothing is cached. On a realistic spec this is orders of magnitude more CPU and allocation per request than the constraint checking itself, and the cost is attacker-selectable: a client simply targets the operation with the largest schema. That is a cheap asymmetric denial of service and a large steady-state throughput loss.
findings.evidence:
func (schema *Schema) useJSONSchema2020(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) error {
        validator, err := newJSONSchemaValidator(schema, settings)   // built per call, line 291
        ...
    }

    func newJSONSchemaValidator(schema *Schema, settings *schemaValidationSettings) (*jsonSchemaValidator, error) {
        schemaBytes, err := json.Marshal(schema)                     // line 22
        var schemaMap map[string]any
        json.Unmarshal(schemaBytes, &schemaMap)                      // line 28
        transformOpenAPIToJSONSchema(schemaMap)                      // full recursive walk, line 33
        compiler := jsonschema.NewCompiler()                         // line 36
        registerFormatValidators(compiler, schemaMap, settings)      // another full recursive walk, line 40
        compiler.AddResource(schemaURL, schemaMap)                   // line 44

findings.title: gorillamux router panics on server URL templates that Validate does not reject
findings.impact: NewRouter dereferences map entries and slices strings without checking, so building a router from a document that was not run through Validate (the function only documents 'Assumes spec is .Validate()d') panics instead of returning an error. Services that build routers from user-supplied or generated specs, or that call NewRouter before Validate, crash. Panicking is also the wrong failure mode for a constructor that already returns an error.

findings.title: SchemaError.Error() panics on values JSON cannot encode; reachable from a YAML request body
findings.impact: Rendering a validation error panics when the rejected value is not JSON-encodable. A request body sent as application/yaml (or application/x-yaml) with a non-string mapping key decodes to map[any]any, which schema validation rejects and stores verbatim in SchemaError.Value; the first call to Error() then panics. The openapi3filter Validator middleware itself formats the error (logFunc does log.Printf("%s: %v", message, err)), so with the shipped middleware the panic is guaranteed, not conditional on application code. Same class of remote denial of service as F-001, and it fires on the error path where most callers have the least defensive code.
findings.evidence:
SchemaError.Error() unconditionally serialises Schema and Value and panics on failure (details are on by default: SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled = false, openapi3/schema.go:34):

    if !SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled {
        ...
        if err := encoder.Encode(err.Schema); err != nil { panic(err) }   // schema.go:3197
        buf.WriteString("\nValue:\n  ")
        if err := encoder.Encode(err.Value); err != nil { panic(err) }    // schema.go:3201
    }

How a non-encodable Value gets there: YamlBodyDecoder is registered by default for application/yaml and application/x-yaml (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1412-1413) and decodes into `any`. yaml3 decodes a mapping whose keys are not all strings into map[any]any. Schema.visitJSON has an explicit case for that type but only converts it when every key is a string:

    case map[any]any:
        values := make(map[string]any, len(value))

findings.title: Default $ref reader performs arbitrary local file reads and unrestricted outbound HTTP with no timeout
findings.impact: Any service that loads an OpenAPI document it did not author - a spec-linting endpoint, a gateway that ingests customer-supplied specs, a CI job on an untrusted PR - exposes two primitives through $ref. ReadFromFile reads any path the process can reach ($ref: "/etc/passwd", or a traversal such as ../../secrets.yaml), and the contents are surfaced back through the parsed document and through error messages. ReadFromHTTP issues a GET to any URL with http.DefaultClient: no scheme or host allowlist, no deny-list for link-local/loopback/RFC1918 targets, no redirect policy, and no timeout at all, which is both a full SSRF primitive (169.254.169.254 cloud metadata, internal admin endpoints) and a resource-exhaustion primitive (a slow-loris server holds a loader goroutine and its buffers open indefinitely).

findings.title: Validator middleware omits the encoded-path-separator check that ValidationHandler performs
findings.impact: The package already recognises that a request whose path contains %2F can resolve to one operation under a router that matches the decoded path and to a different operation under a router that matches the escaped path; ValidationHandler rejects such requests precisely because 'the operation validated here - its security requirements included - would not be the operation the wrapped handler serves'. The newer Validator.Middleware, which is the wrapper most integrations use, performs no such check: it calls FindRoute and validates whatever operation that returns, then passes the untouched request to the wrapped handler. When the embedding application routes on a different normalisation than the router given to the Validator (kin's own two routers already differ: routers/gorillamux uses mux.UseEncodedPath, routers/legacy matches req.URL.Path), a request can be validated against a permissive operation and served by a protected one - i.e. the security requirements and schemas of the wrong operation are enforced.

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi openai3filter: nil-pointer panic in ConvertErrors on malformed multipart/form-data body enables unauthenticated DoS
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

A nil-pointer dereference in `openapi3filter.ConvertErrors` lets any unauthenticated client crash a server with a single HTTP request. When an application validates a `multipart/form-data` request body and renders the resulting validation error through the library-provided `ValidationErrorEncoder` / `ConvertErrors` helpers, a malformed scalar form field (e.g. a non-numeric value for an `integer` property) produces an error shape that `convertParseError` dereferences without a nil check. The handler goroutine panics, causing a denial of service. `application/json` request bodies are **not** affected — the bug is specific to `multipart/form-data`.

The panic is in `convertParseError`, at [`openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go:119-120`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/validation_error_encoder.go#L119) (still present on `master` at the time of writing):
